passage: The monsoon had come through the ground floor of Preeti's building overnight, and by morning the lobby held about a foot of brown water and somebody's floating slipper. Preeti waded out in her office shoes, holding her bag over her head, and met Vijay at the gate. He was carrying a bucket and looking at his ruined scooter. "How's the commute?" he asked. Preeti considered the water lapping at her knees. "Slightly damp," she said. Vijay burst out laughing. "I heard the lift is having a small moment too." They both knew the lift was underwater. Preeti still had a shaky hand on her bag strap, and Vijay noticed, and handed her the bucket to hold instead. 🙂

qa.q: What did Preeti call the flood on her commute?
qa.a: She said it was "slightly damp".

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling under her joke, and what shows it?
qa.a: Under the calm joke she was likely shaken and coping, shown by the shaky hand on her bag strap, though she may also have been amused.

qa.q: What could Vijay do next to help Preeti after the joke?
qa.a: He could offer practical help, like carrying her bag or making tea, and ask later how she is really doing.

qa.q: How does Vijay understand Preeti's understatement?
qa.a: He knows how bad the flood is, so he sees the dry line as coping and joins in with his own understatement about the lift.

grounding: Preeti uses dry understatement about a flood, which works because Vijay shares the sense of the real scale.

passage:
"How was the presentation?" Simran asked, dropping her keys on the flat's counter.
"Not my best day," Maria said from the sofa. Her laptop had died mid-slide, the projector had shut off twice, and she'd spilled coffee on her professor's handout.
"That sounds a bit more than not your best."
"Well, the coffee did add some colour."
Simran snorted. "Did the professor say anything?"
"He said I 'recovered gracefully.' I think he was being kind." Maria pulled a cushion over her face. "I'm fine. Mostly."
Simran sat beside her. "Mostly is allowed. Do you want to keep joking, or talk properly?"
Maria peeked out. "Joking for ten more minutes, then talking."
"Deal."

qa.q: What did the professor say about Maria's recovery?
qa.a: He said she 'recovered gracefully'.

qa.q: What does Maria's phrase 'not my best day' tell you about how she is coping, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests she is using understatement to cope with an awful day, though she may also be hiding how upset she is, which her 'mostly' hints at.

qa.q: What did Simran do that helped?
qa.a: She played along with the joke, then gently asked if Maria wanted to keep joking or talk, so Maria could choose.

qa.q: How might Simran see Maria's understatement?
qa.a: Simran knows the presentation went badly, so she reads the understatement as coping but still checks, in case Maria needs more than a joke.

grounding: Maria's comic understatement conveys coping and works because Simran shares the sense of how bad it was.

passage: I still laugh about the night our hostel flooded in Chennai. I'm Yusuf. The rain came through the window at 2 a.m., and by morning there was water up to our ankles, my mattress floating, and my laptop sitting on top of the cupboard where I'd flung it. My roommate Varun, standing in the doorway in his shorts, looked at the whole mess and said, "It's slightly damp." I lost it. I laughed so much I sat down in the water. And somehow, after that, it didn't feel like a disaster. We fished out our books, hung the clothes on the stair railings, and I kept saying "slightly damp" all day. The warden didn't find it as funny. When she asked how our room was, Varun said, "Bit breezy," and she just stared at him. She hadn't seen the room. We had to show her.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf fling the laptop?
qa.a: On top of the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Varun said "It's slightly damp"?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a burst of amusement that eased the stress, laughing so hard that the flood stopped feeling like a disaster.

qa.q: Why did Varun's joke work with Yusuf but not with the warden?
qa.a: Yusuf could see the real mess, so the understatement read as coping; the warden hadn't seen the room, so she didn't get the irony.

qa.q: How did the warden react to "Bit breezy"?
qa.a: She just stared, probably confused or unamused, since she didn't know the true scale of the flood.

grounding: Shows a young adult using dry understatement to cope with a flood, and how the joke depends on shared understanding of the true scale.

passage:
Coach's note, college hockey team, after Saturday's match.
We lost 0–6 to the university team. It was a hard afternoon; the boys were quiet in the dressing room, heads down. Anirban, our goalkeeper, who had faced about thirty shots, took off his pads, looked around and said, "Well. Not our finest hour." There was a pause, and then Madhav laughed, then everyone did. I watched the room loosen. Anirban's understatement worked because everyone knew exactly how bad it had been; it said "we all saw it, and we're still here". I noticed he was the one who had most reason to feel low, and he chose that line. Later, in the bus, I asked him privately how he was really doing. He said, "Honestly? Gutted. But I didn't want everyone sulking." I told him I appreciated it, and that he could be gutted with me too. We'll review the match on Tuesday.
— Coach Mehra

qa.q: What was the score of Saturday's match?
What was Anirban feeling after the match, beneath the joke?
qa.a: He felt gutted and deeply disappointed, as he told the coach, but chose the understatement to lift the team.

qa.q: What did the coach do that was wise after the joke?
qa.a: The coach checked privately on Anirban, recognising that the humour might cover real disappointment, and invited him to share it.

qa.q: How did the team experience Anirban's line?
qa.a: After a pause, Madhav laughed and then everyone did, and the room loosened because they all knew how bad it had been.

grounding: Shows a young adult using dry understatement after a heavy loss to cope and connect, relying on shared knowledge of the true scale.

passage:
Monday night.
Interview day. The scooter broke down in the pouring rain two kilometres from the office. I pushed it into a petrol pump, got into an auto, the auto got a flat tyre, and I walked the last bit with my file inside my kurta so the certificates wouldn't get soaked. Walked in dripping, eleven minutes late.
Afterwards I sat in a café and texted Yash: "Not my best day." Yash replied: "Uh oh. How not-best? Scale of 1 to monsoon?" I laughed for the first time all day. Told the whole story. Yash said, "You still went in, though. Dripping. That's a story they'll remember."
And the funny thing is, the panel did smile when I said, "Sorry, the weather had other plans." One of them said, "Clearly." Waiting to hear back. Changing into dry socks now.
— Vasudha

qa.q: How late was Vasudha for the interview?
qa.a: Eleven minutes late.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when texting "Not my best day"?
qa.a: Vasudha felt frustrated and worn out, using understatement to cope, and then relieved when Yash's reply made Vasudha laugh.

qa.q: Why did Yash's reply work so well?
qa.a: Yash understood the understatement and played along with humour, then encouraged Vasudha by pointing out the courage of going in anyway.

qa.q: How did the interview panel seem to receive Vasudha's line about the weather?
qa.a: They smiled, and one said "Clearly", showing they understood the understatement because they could see how soaked Vasudha was.

grounding: Shows a young adult using dry understatement to cope with a disastrous day, relying on others understanding the true scale.
